l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Grant Munro asks Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson to investigate why his wife, Effie, secretly visits a cottage at Norbury where a strange face appears at the window. Holmes suspects that Effie's first husband or his associates are blackmailing her, but the cottage is inhabited by an old nurse and Effie's daughter, Lucy, whose face has been covered by a mask. Effie reveals that Lucy is her child by her deceased first husband, John Hebron, an African American man, and that she concealed the child because she feared losing Grant. Grant accepts Effie and Lucy, and Holmes later uses “Norbury” as a reminder not to become overconfident.

l: Grant Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Grant Munro becomes convinced that his wife is concealing a serious secret in the cottage at Norbury. He forces his way inside with Holmes and Watson, learns that the supposed strange occupant is his wife’s daughter, Lucy, and responds by kissing and carrying the child home while offering Effie his hand.

l: Effie Munro, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Effie secretly visits the cottage because she wants to see her daughter Lucy, whom she has kept hidden from Grant. She explains that fear of losing Grant caused her to conceal Lucy, and she asks what will become of herself and her child after the secret is exposed.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the cottage mystery and initially theorizes that Effie’s first husband or his associates are blackmailing her. He discovers that the livid face belongs to a masked child and later admits that the case should remind him not to become overconfident.

l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Dr. Watson listens to Grant Munro’s account, accompanies Holmes and Grant to the cottage, and witnesses the revelation of Lucy’s identity. He initially finds the strange face horrifying but then laughs when the mask is removed.

l: Lucy, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Lucy is Effie’s daughter by John Hebron and has been living in the cottage under the care of a former servant. She is a little black girl dressed in a red frock and white gloves, and her face has been covered to conceal her racial identity from the neighbours.

l: John Hebron, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: John Hebron was Effie’s first husband in Atlanta and the father of Lucy. Effie describes him as a noble and handsome man of African descent who had died before the events of this unit.

l: the cottage near Grant Munro's house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: The cottage appears deserted when Grant first enters it, but later it is shown to be occupied by an old woman and Lucy. Its comfortable upper room contains Effie’s photograph and becomes the place where Effie’s hidden child and her secret are revealed.

l: Norbury, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Norbury is the location of Grant and Effie’s home and the mysterious cottage. Holmes later tells Watson that the word “Norbury” should be used to remind him of this case if he becomes overconfident.

l: mystery concerning Jack's wife and the cottage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: The secret is that Effie has arranged for her daughter Lucy to stay in the cottage under the care of a nurse. Effie has concealed Lucy from Grant because she feared that he would reject her child because of Lucy’s African ancestry.

l: blackmail, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Holmes initially believes that blackmail explains Effie’s secrecy, the hundred pounds she sent, and her efforts to prevent Grant from entering the cottage. This theory proves mistaken when Effie reveals that the money was sent to Lucy’s nurse.

l: Effie and Grant Munro's marriage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Effie’s concealment of Lucy creates the first serious shadow between her and Grant. After the truth is revealed, Grant indicates that he will accept Effie and Lucy and discuss the matter more comfortably at home.

l: the revelation of Lucy's identity, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Lucy’s identity is revealed when Holmes removes the mask from the livid face at the window and exposes a little black girl. Effie then explains that Lucy is her daughter, born to her and John Hebron.

s: A full-length photograph of Effie stands on the mantelpiece in the cottage’s comfortable room. Effie had given the photograph to the nurse as part of the arrangements for Lucy’s stay.

s: The face at the window appears unnaturally coloured and rigid, vanishing with a jerk whenever Grant approaches. It is later explained as Lucy’s masked face, deliberately covered so that neighbours would not see that she was a black child.

l: the mask on Lucy's face, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Lucy wears a mask that makes her face appear livid and expressionless, creating the frightening apparition seen by Grant. Holmes removes it by passing his hand behind her ear, revealing Lucy’s true face.

l: racial identity and prejudice, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared
s: Effie explains that she married John Hebron despite his African descent and that Lucy inherited a much darker appearance from her father. Effie concealed Lucy because she feared Grant would reject her, while Grant’s final acceptance shows that he does not abandon Effie or the child after learning the truth.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Dr. John Watson, now running a medical practice in Paddington, joins Sherlock Holmes on a journey to Birmingham to investigate Hall Pycroft’s strange employment experience. Pycroft describes losing his position at Coxon & Woodhouse before receiving a lucrative job offer from Arthur Pinner to become business manager of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. Arthur sends Pycroft to Birmingham with £100 and a written agreement, where Harry Pinner supposedly confirms the appointment and assigns him work compiling lists from a Paris directory. Pycroft realizes that Arthur and Harry are the same man and asks Holmes to explain why he was sent from London to Birmingham.

l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Dr. John Watson is visited by Sherlock Holmes shortly after taking over a medical practice in Paddington. He accompanies Holmes and Hall Pycroft to Birmingham and listens as Pycroft recounts the suspicious job offer.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Sherlock Holmes deduces from Watson’s scorched slippers that Watson recently had a severe chill. He takes Watson to Birmingham to investigate Hall Pycroft’s case and recognizes that the two supposed Pinner brothers are the same man because they share the same voice, figure, and identically stuffed tooth.

l: Hall Pycroft, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Hall Pycroft is a former clerk of Coxon & Woodhouse who is offered a position at Mawson & Williams after the collapse of his former firm. He is persuaded by Arthur Pinner to accept a much higher-paying position with the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, receives £100, and is sent to Birmingham, where he becomes suspicious after meeting the supposed Harry Pinner.

l: Arthur Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Arthur Pinner visits Hall Pycroft in London and praises his financial ability, offering him the position of business manager of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, at a salary of £500 plus commission. He gives Pycroft a £100 advance, obtains a written agreement, and directs him to meet his supposed brother in Birmingham.

l: Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Harry Pinner supposedly meets Hall Pycroft at 126B Corporation Street in Birmingham and confirms his engagement with the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. He assigns Pycroft the task of marking hardware sellers in a Paris directory and later asks him to list furniture shops; Holmes and Pycroft conclude that Harry is actually Arthur Pinner in disguise.

l: Mawson & Williams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Mawson & Williams is a wealthy stockbroking firm in Lombard Street that offers Hall Pycroft a clerkship paying £200 a year. Arthur Pinner tries to persuade Pycroft not to resign from the firm.

l: the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: The Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, is presented to Hall Pycroft as a company with 134 branches in France, plus one in Brussels and one in San Remo. Its supposed temporary offices in Birmingham are sparsely furnished and have no company name displayed.

l: Birmingham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Birmingham is where Hall Pycroft is directed to report for his new employment. He meets the supposed Harry Pinner there at 126B Corporation Street and is given work compiling commercial lists.

l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: London is where Hall Pycroft receives the offer from Arthur Pinner and where Mawson & Williams is located. Pycroft returns to London by night train to consult Sherlock Holmes after becoming suspicious in Birmingham.

l: 126B Corporation Street, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: 126B Corporation Street in Birmingham is given to Hall Pycroft as the temporary office address of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. The address consists of a passage leading to offices, but no company name appears on the wall.

l: Pycroft's £100 advance, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: Arthur Pinner gives Hall Pycroft a £100 advance on his supposed salary. Pycroft keeps the money while working on the lists in Birmingham, despite his growing doubts about the company.

l: Pycroft's written agreement, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: At Arthur Pinner’s request, Hall Pycroft writes that he is perfectly willing to act as business manager of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, at a minimum salary of £500. Arthur puts the written agreement in his pocket.

l: Paris directory, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: The supposed Harry Pinner gives Hall Pycroft a large Paris directory and orders him to mark all hardware sellers and their addresses. After Pycroft completes that task, Pinner asks him to compile a list of furniture shops as well.

l: Franco-Midland job offer, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: The Franco-Midland job offer promises Hall Pycroft the position of business manager, a starting salary of £500, and one percent commission on business conducted by his agents. The offer leads Pycroft away from the safer position at Mawson & Williams and sends him to Birmingham.

l: hardware trade, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk
s: The supposed company is described as intending to purchase English crockery and distribute it through agents and branches in France. Hall Pycroft is asked to identify hardware sellers and furniture shops in Paris as part of this purported trade.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and Hall Pycroft visit Arthur Harry Pinner at the temporary offices of the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, where Pinner attempts to hang himself after seeing them. Holmes deduces that Pinner and his brother obtained Pycroft’s handwriting so one brother could impersonate him at Mawson & Williams. An Evening Standard report reveals that the impersonator, Beddington, attempted to rob Mawson & Williams, murdered its watchman, and was captured with stolen securities. Pinner’s suicide attempt is explained as his response to learning that his brother’s crime had been exposed.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Sherlock Holmes visits Arthur Harry Pinner with Dr. John Watson and Hall Pycroft, questions the circumstances, and breaks into the inner room when Pinner begins choking himself. He deduces that Pycroft’s handwriting was obtained for imitation and that one of the criminals impersonated Pycroft at Mawson & Williams; he later recognizes the Evening Standard report as explaining Pinner’s suicide attempt.

l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Hall Pycroft to the temporary company offices. He helps rescue Arthur Harry Pinner, examines him, treats him with water and artificial movement, and reads aloud the Evening Standard report about the attempted robbery at Mawson & Williams.

l: Hall Pycroft, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Hall Pycroft brings Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson to meet Arthur Harry Pinner and explains the arrangements connected with the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited. He learns that his handwriting was obtained so that another man could impersonate him at Mawson & Williams, and he is sent to contact the police after the robbery is revealed.

l: Arthur Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Arthur Harry Pinner is found in a state of extreme terror at the temporary company offices and asks to be left alone. He enters an inner room and attempts to hang himself with his braces, but Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and Hall Pycroft rescue him; he later explains that the newspaper report is the reason for his action.

l: Beddington, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Beddington is identified in the Evening Standard as the criminal who used the false name Hall Pycroft to obtain employment at Mawson & Williams. He obtained mouldings of locks and knowledge of the strong room, murdered the watchman, stole securities, and was captured while leaving with a carpet bag.

l: Beddington's brother, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Beddington's brother worked with him in the scheme and impersonated Hall Pycroft at Mawson & Williams. He is identified with Arthur Harry Pinner, who attempts suicide after learning that Beddington has been captured and that the crime has been exposed.

l: the Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: The Franco-Midland Hardware Company, Limited, is presented as the company for which Arthur Harry Pinner claims to be managing director. Its supposed employment arrangements are used to obtain Hall Pycroft’s handwriting, keep him away from London, and support the impersonation scheme.

l: Mawson & Williams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Mawson & Williams is the financial house where the false Hall Pycroft obtains a clerk’s position. It holds securities worth considerably more than a million pounds, and Beddington uses his position there to prepare an attempted robbery.

l: London, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: London is where Mawson & Williams is located and where the attempted robbery, murder of the watchman, and capture of Beddington take place. The conspirators keep Hall Pycroft in the Midlands to prevent him from returning to London and discovering the impersonation.

l: the temporary company offices, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: The temporary company offices are a bare, unfurnished set of rooms on the fifth floor. Arthur Harry Pinner meets Hall Pycroft, Sherlock Holmes, and Dr. John Watson there, then attempts to hang himself in an inner room.

l: the Evening Standard, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: The Evening Standard carries an early report titled “Crime in the City. Murder at Mawson & Williams,” describing the attempted robbery, the murder of the watchman, and the capture of Beddington. Its report explains to Holmes and the others why Arthur Harry Pinner attempted suicide.

l: the attempted robbery at Mawson & Williams, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: The attempted robbery at Mawson & Williams involves Beddington using a false identity to gain access to the firm, learn about its safes, and steal securities. He is intercepted while leaving with nearly a hundred thousand pounds’ worth of American railway bonds and other scrip.

l: the murder of the watchman, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: The watchman at Mawson & Williams is murdered by a blow from a poker delivered from behind. His body is hidden inside the largest safe and is discovered after Beddington is stopped.

l: Harry Pinner, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Arthur Harry Pinner's suicide attempt occurs immediately after he meets Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and Hall Pycroft at the temporary company offices. He hangs himself with his braces but is found in time and revived by the three men.

l: the capture of Beddington, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: The capture of Beddington occurs after Sergeant Tuson follows him from Mawson & Williams and, with Constable Pollock, overcomes his resistance. Beddington is found carrying stolen securities in a carpet bag.

l: handwriting imitation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: Handwriting imitation is central to the scheme because the criminals obtain Hall Pycroft’s written declaration as a specimen. One of them learns to copy his writing so that an impersonator can take Pycroft’s expected position at Mawson & Williams without immediate suspicion.

l: the impersonation of Hall Pycroft, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his
s: The impersonation of Hall Pycroft allows Beddington to obtain a clerk’s position at Mawson & Williams under Pycroft’s name. The real Pycroft is kept away from London by promises of employment and an advance, while the false Pycroft studies the premises and prepares the robbery.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Sherlock Holmes tells Dr. Watson about the case of the Gloria Scott, which was the first criminal investigation in which Holmes was involved. As a college student, Holmes visited Donnithorpe and observed that Victor Trevor's father, Mr. Trevor, feared a past connection involving the sailor Hudson and another man named Beddoes. Hudson gained power over Mr. Trevor, and a strange coded message sent from Hampshire caused Mr. Trevor to suffer a fatal stroke. Holmes determines that every third word of the message, beginning with the first, contains a warning that explains Mr. Trevor's terror.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Sherlock Holmes recounts his first criminal case to Dr. Watson. During his visit to Donnithorpe, he deduces details about Mr. Trevor's past from his appearance and later recognizes that the strange message contains a hidden meaning.

l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Dr. Watson listens as Sherlock Holmes explains the case of the Gloria Scott and examines the papers and coded message Holmes shows him.

l: Victor Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Victor Trevor was Sherlock Holmes's only friend during his two years at college and invited him to Donnithorpe. He later summoned Holmes back when his father was dying and explained how Hudson had gained control over the household.

l: Mr. Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Mr. Trevor was Victor Trevor's father, a wealthy landowner, Justice of the Peace, and former traveler and gold-digger. He had a half-effaced tattoo bearing the initials J. A., feared a past connection, and fell under Hudson's power before suffering a fatal stroke after receiving a coded message.

l: Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Hudson was a sailor who had known Mr. Trevor and Mr. Beddoes many years earlier. After returning to Mr. Trevor's house, he obtained employment there, behaved abusively, and appeared to use knowledge of the past to control Mr. Trevor.

l: Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: The Gloria Scott is the subject of the extraordinary case documented in the papers Sherlock Holmes shows Dr. Watson.

l: the case of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: The case of the Gloria Scott was the first case in which Sherlock Holmes was ever engaged. Its documents concern Mr. Trevor's past, Hudson's threats, and the coded message that preceded Mr. Trevor's death.

l: the warning message, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: The coded message appeared to discuss game, a head-keeper, fly-paper, and a hen-pheasant's life. Sherlock Holmes realizes that reading every third word, beginning with the first, reveals a threatening message capable of explaining Mr. Trevor's terror.

l: the secret code, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: The secret code hides a second meaning in an apparently trivial and grotesque message. Sherlock Holmes discovers that the message is deciphered by taking every third word, beginning with the first.

l: the secret held over the men by Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: The guilty secret appears to involve Mr. Trevor, Hudson, and Mr. Beddoes, who had been associated in the past. Holmes believes Hudson may have threatened to expose it or that Beddoes may have warned Mr. Trevor about such an exposure.

l: Donnithorpe, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Donnithorpe was the Norfolk home of Mr. Trevor and Victor Trevor, where Sherlock Holmes spent part of the long vacation. Hudson later lived and acted abusively within the household there.

l: the papers concerning the Gloria Scott case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: The papers concerning the Gloria Scott case were kept in the back drawer of the Japanese cabinet. Victor Trevor retrieved them after his father's death and gave them to Sherlock Holmes.

l: Mr. Trevor's death, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Mr. Trevor died shortly after suffering a stroke caused by the coded message. Before his death, he briefly regained consciousness and said that the papers were in the back drawer of the Japanese cabinet.

l: Mr. Trevor's stroke, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: Mr. Trevor suffered a stroke immediately after reading a letter bearing the Fordingbridge postmark. The paralysis spread, he did not regain consciousness except briefly before his death, and the letter was later understood to contain a hidden warning.

l: the threat and blackmail, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, V. The “_Gloria Scott_”
s: The text suggests that Hudson used knowledge of the guilty secret to blackmail or otherwise control Mr. Trevor. Victor Trevor also believed Hudson might have intended to blackmail Mr. Beddoes.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: The warning message tells Victor Trevor that Hudson has revealed everything and that he must flee for his life. Holmes explains that the message uses a prearranged cipher and infers from its sporting terms that Beddoes likely sent it. Victor recalls that his father received invitations from Beddoes to shoot over his preserves. Victor then gives Holmes a statement written by his father about the danger posed by Hudson and asks Holmes to read it aloud.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: Holmes explains how the warning message's prearranged cipher works and infers that its sporting vocabulary suggests the sender is an ardent shot or interested in breeding. He asks Victor whether he knows anything about Beddoes and concludes that Beddoes sent the note.

l: Victor Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: Victor is distressed by the warning, believing that its meaning involves disgrace as well as danger. He recalls his father's invitations from Beddoes to shoot over his preserves and gives Holmes his father's statement, asking Holmes to read it because he lacks the strength and courage to do so himself.

l: Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: Hudson is identified in the warning as having told all. He is described as a sailor who held a secret over the heads of two wealthy and respected men, including Victor Trevor's father.

l: Beddoes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: Beddoes is identified by Holmes as the likely sender of the warning because of its sporting references. Victor recalls that Beddoes used to invite his father to shoot over his preserves every autumn.

l: Victor Trevor's father, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: Victor Trevor's father received autumn invitations from Beddoes to shoot over his preserves. He wrote a statement when the danger from Hudson became imminent, and Victor found it in the Japanese cabinet.

l: the warning message, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: The warning says, "The game is up. Hudson has told all. Fly for your life." It uses a prearranged cipher in which the writer fills spaces with two additional words, including the sporting terms "head-keepers" and "hen pheasants."

l: the statement drawn up by Victor Trevor's father, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: The statement was written by Victor Trevor's father when Hudson's danger had become imminent. Victor found it in the Japanese cabinet and hands it to Holmes to read aloud.

l: the secret held over the men by Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my
s: The secret is described as something that Hudson held over the heads of two wealthy and respected men. Victor fears that it concerns sin and shame, but its nature is not revealed in this unit.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The unit concerns papers read to Watson, including a letter in which Trevor reveals that his real name is James Armitage. He describes meeting Jack Prendergast, who had organized a conspiracy involving prisoners, the crew, the chaplain, two warders, and the second mate to seize the ship. The conspirators secretly obtained weapons and planned a nighttime attack before events forced the plot to begin sooner than expected.

l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: Watson is present as the papers are read aloud to him. The papers include a letter describing James Armitage's past and the voyage of the Gloria Scott.

l: James Armitage, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: James Armitage says that he formerly used the name Trevor. He was convicted of breaking the law after using money that was not his own to pay a debt of honour, and he was sentenced to transportation aboard the Gloria Scott.

l: Victor Trevor, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: Trevor is revealed to be the name James Armitage used later in life. The letter is addressed by Trevor to his son and explains his former identity and conviction.

l: Jack Prendergast, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: Jack Prendergast is a very tall convict and the leader of a plot to gain command of the Gloria Scott. He had obtained large sums of money through fraud, retained money that was not recovered, and used it to recruit the crew and others to the conspiracy.

l: Wilson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The chaplain is described as a partner in Prendergast's plan. He is secretly a sham chaplain who comes aboard with correct papers, money, and a black bag, and he has bought the loyalty of the crew, two warders, and the second mate.

l: Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The Gloria Scott is an old five-hundred-ton vessel formerly used in the Chinese tea trade and later used to transport convicts. It carries thirty-eight convicts, twenty-six crew members, eighteen soldiers, officers, a doctor, a chaplain, and four warders.

l: Watson's papers, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: Watson's papers are read aloud and are endorsed with particulars of the voyage of the bark Gloria Scott from its departure from Falmouth to its destruction. They contain the letter in which James Armitage recounts his past and the events aboard the ship.

l: letter about the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The letter is written by Trevor to his son. It states that Trevor's real name is James Armitage and records his conviction, transportation, and involvement in the events aboard the Gloria Scott.

l: the voyage of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The voyage begins with the Gloria Scott leaving Falmouth on October 8, 1855, carrying nearly one hundred people toward Australia. During the voyage, the prisoners receive weapons, organize a conspiracy, and prepare to seize the ship.

l: the destruction of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The papers are endorsed as covering the destruction of the Gloria Scott on November 6, in north latitude 15º 20’ and west longitude 25º 14’. This unit has not yet described the destruction itself.

l: transportation to Australia, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: James Armitage is sentenced to transportation to Australia after his conviction. He is carried there aboard the Gloria Scott with thirty-seven other convicts.

l: James Armitage's conviction, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: James Armitage is convicted of breaking his country's laws after using money entrusted to him to pay a debt of honour. He receives the sentence of transportation and is placed aboard the Gloria Scott on his twenty-third birthday.

l: the conspiracy to seize the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The conspiracy is organized before the prisoners come aboard, with Jack Prendergast as its leader and his money as its motive power. Its members obtain pistols, powder, files, and slugs, recruit the crew and others, and plan a sudden nighttime attack.

l: the prisoners, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The prisoners include thirty-eight convicts transported aboard the Gloria Scott. Nearly all join the conspiracy after receiving weapons, except for one prisoner considered mentally weak and another suffering from jaundice.

l: the conspirators, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The conspirators include Prendergast, many of the prisoners, the sham chaplain, two warders, Mercer the second mate, and the crew. They conceal weapons in their cells and prepare to attack the opposing officers, soldiers, warders, and doctor.

l: the crew of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: The crew are described as ruffians specially picked for the conspiracy. Prendergast's partner, posing as the chaplain, buys their loyalty before they sign on.

l: Australia, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “These are the very papers, Watson, which he handed to me, and I
s: Australia is the destination to which James Armitage and the other convicts are being transported aboard the Gloria Scott.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: The narrative describes the mutiny aboard the transport ship Gloria Scott, in which the prisoners and some sailors seize the vessel and massacre most of its officers and soldiers. Prendergast leads the surviving mutineers, while Evans and others refuse to participate in the execution of the remaining prisoners and escape in a boat. The Gloria Scott is destroyed when the first mate threatens to ignite a powder barrel and an explosion kills those aboard. Years later, Evans and Beddoes are threatened and blackmailed by Hudson, a sailor who survived the wreck, but all three men ultimately disappear.

l: Jack Prendergast, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: Prendergast leads the mutiny after the prisoners break free, killing soldiers and insisting that the remaining warders, mates, and doctor must be silenced. He refuses to spare them, permits Evans and seven others to leave in a boat, and later kills the surgeon before the first mate causes the Gloria Scott to explode.

l: Evans, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: Evans participates in the mutiny but refuses, with seven others, to approve the cold-blooded killing of the surviving officers and warders. He escapes in a boat, is picked up by the brig Hotspur, changes his name in Sydney, and later becomes wealthy with Beddoes. He recognizes Hudson as the sailor rescued from the wreck and fears Hudson's threats.

l: Hudson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: Hudson is a young seaman who survives the destruction of the Gloria Scott by clinging to wreckage and is rescued by Evans and the others. Years later, he tracks down Evans and Beddoes and lives upon their fears by threatening to expose their past. He and Beddoes eventually disappear.

l: Beddoes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: Beddoes is one of the men involved in the mutiny and later changes his name with Evans after reaching Sydney. He becomes wealthy and lives peacefully for more than twenty years before Hudson threatens to reveal their past. A cipher warns that Hudson has told all; Beddoes then disappears, probably after killing Hudson and fleeing with money.

l: the prisoners, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: The prisoners are held aboard the Gloria Scott and help carry out the mutiny after the doctor discovers hidden pistols. Most of them participate in the fighting and subsequent massacre, while Evans and four other convicts refuse to support the killing of the remaining prisoners and leave in a boat.

l: the prisoners, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: The convicts overpower the guards and soldiers, seize weapons, and take control of the Gloria Scott. Some convicts join Prendergast in killing the remaining officers, while five convicts, including Evans, reject the executions and escape. A group of convicts later confronts the first mate beside an open powder barrel, triggering the ship's destruction.

l: Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: The Gloria Scott is a transport ship carrying prisoners that is captured during a violent mutiny. After the escape boat leaves, the ship's first mate threatens to blow it up using a powder barrel, and an explosion destroys the vessel and nearly everyone aboard. The Admiralty records it as lost at sea without learning its true fate.

l: the transport-ship mutiny and massacre, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: The mutiny begins when the doctor discovers pistols hidden beneath a prisoner's bunk. The mutineers shoot the sentries, soldiers, and captain, then massacre many of the remaining prisoners and officers; the violence causes a dispute when Evans and seven others refuse to support further executions.

l: the escape from the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: Evans and seven others leave the Gloria Scott in a boat after refusing to participate in the planned executions. They receive sailors' clothing, provisions, a compass, and a false account describing them as shipwrecked mariners, then head toward Sierra Leone before seeing the Gloria Scott explode.

l: the destruction of the Gloria Scott, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: The first mate escapes his bonds and hides beside an open powder barrel in the after-hold, threatening to blow up the ship if attacked. An explosion follows, possibly caused by a convict's misdirected bullet rather than the mate's match, destroying the Gloria Scott and killing the mutineers and remaining people aboard except for Hudson.

l: the threat and blackmail, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “‘One evening, about the third week after our start, the doctor
s: Hudson tracks down Evans and Beddoes decades after the mutiny and threatens to expose their involvement in the Gloria Scott. Evans tries to keep the peace because of the danger, but a warning says that Hudson has told all; Hudson and Beddoes then disappear, with the narrator believing that Beddoes killed Hudson and fled.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Sherlock Holmes tells Dr. John Watson about the Musgrave Ritual case, an early investigation that helped establish his professional reputation. Reginald Musgrave asks Holmes to investigate the disappearance of his butler, Brunton, and the subsequent disappearance of Rachel Howells at Hurlstone. Brunton had been caught studying the family’s ritual document, while Rachel’s footprints led to the mere, where a linen bag containing rusted metal and dull pebbles was recovered. Holmes begins by asking to examine the ritual document.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Sherlock Holmes recounts the Musgrave Ritual case to Dr. John Watson. He is consulted by Reginald Musgrave after Brunton and Rachel Howells disappear, and he begins investigating by asking to see the ritual document.

l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Dr. John Watson listens as Sherlock Holmes describes the Musgrave Ritual case and its connection to Holmes’s early professional work. He had heard Holmes mention the case before but did not know its details.

l: the Musgrave Ritual, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The Musgrave Ritual is a private family observance performed by each Musgrave on coming of age. It is considered ancient and of possible archaeological interest, though Reginald Musgrave initially regards it as having no practical use.

l: Reginald Musgrave, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Reginald Musgrave is a former college acquaintance of Sherlock Holmes and a member of an old family established at Hurlstone in western Sussex. He asks Holmes to investigate strange events at Hurlstone after Brunton and Rachel Howells disappear.

l: Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Brunton is the long-serving butler at Hurlstone, known for his intelligence, languages, musical ability, and womanizing. Reginald Musgrave catches him secretly studying a copy of the Musgrave Ritual and dismisses him, after which Brunton disappears from the house, leaving his clothes, watch, and money behind.

l: Rachel Howells, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Rachel Howells is the second housemaid at Hurlstone who had been engaged to Brunton before he abandoned her for Janet Tregellis. After Brunton’s disappearance she becomes ill and hysterical, then vanishes from her room; her footprints lead to the mere, but her body is not found.

l: Hurlstone, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Hurlstone is the Musgrave family estate in western Sussex. Strange events there include Brunton’s secret examination of the ritual document, his disappearance, and Rachel Howells’s disappearance.

l: the Musgrave Ritual case, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The Musgrave Ritual case is one of Sherlock Holmes’s early investigations and is described as a singular chain of events with unusually large issues at stake. It concerns the ritual document, Brunton’s disappearance, Rachel Howells’s disappearance, and the objects recovered from the mere.

l: the ritual document, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The ritual document is a copy of the questions and answers used in the Musgrave family’s ancient observance. Brunton secretly removes it from a bureau and studies it in the library, prompting Reginald Musgrave to dismiss him; Holmes asks to examine it.

l: the library, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The library at Hurlstone is where Reginald Musgrave discovers Brunton late at night. Brunton is sitting there with a chart-like paper and secretly studies the ritual document by the light of a taper.

l: the mere, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The mere is the lake on the Hurlstone grounds, which is eight feet deep. Rachel Howells’s footprints lead to its edge, and a search there recovers a linen bag, though no body is found.

l: the linen bag, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The linen bag is recovered from the mere during the search for Rachel Howells. It contains rusted and discoloured metal along with several dull-coloured pieces of pebble or glass.

l: the rusted metal and dull pebbles, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The rusted metal and dull pebbles are found inside the linen bag recovered from the mere. Their nature is not explained in this unit.

l: the Hurlstone house, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The Hurlstone house is a rambling old building with a labyrinthine original wing that is largely uninhabited. Brunton disappears from it despite its doors and windows being found fastened, and the house is searched without revealing his whereabouts.

l: the disappearance of Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: The disappearance of Brunton occurs after he is ordered to leave Hurlstone within a week for secretly examining the ritual document. He is last seen before retiring to his room, and afterward his clothes, watch, and money remain there while his black suit and slippers are missing.

l: Howells's disappearance, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VI. The Musgrave Ritual
s: Rachel Howells disappears from her room on the third night after Brunton’s disappearance while a nurse is watching over her. Her open window and footprints lead toward the mere, but neither she nor her body is found.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: Musgrave shows Watson a paper containing the Musgrave catechism, a seventeenth-century family text of questions and answers. The catechism concerns ownership, succession, the positions of the sun and shadow, a sequence of steps, and a trust. Holmes believes the paper is practical and that Brunton had consulted it while comparing it with a map or chart. Holmes and Musgrave plan to travel to Sussex to investigate the mystery on the spot.

l: Reginald Musgrave, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: Musgrave gives Watson the paper containing the catechism and reads its questions and answers. He says the original has no date but uses the spelling of the middle of the seventeenth century, and he initially doubts that it can help solve the mystery.

l: Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: Holmes believes Brunton had previously seen the Musgrave catechism and consulted it on the night Musgrave caught him. Brunton apparently compared it with some map or chart, which he put into his pocket when Musgrave appeared.

l: Musgrave family, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: The Musgrave family preserved the catechism, which each Musgrave had to answer when he came to man's estate. The original is written in spelling associated with the middle of the seventeenth century.

l: Sussex, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: Holmes proposes that he and Musgrave take the first train to Sussex to investigate the matter more deeply at the location.

l: paper containing the Musgrave catechism, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: Musgrave has the paper with him and shows it to Watson. It contains the catechism, has no date, and is written in the spelling of the middle of the seventeenth century.

l: Musgrave catechism, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: The catechism asks whose possession something belonged to, who will receive it, where the sun and shadow were, how it was stepped, what should be given for it, and why it should be given. Its answers refer to the person who is gone, the person who will come, the oak, the elm, a sequence of directional steps, all that is owned, and the sake of the trust.

l: map or chart, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: Brunton apparently had a map or chart that he compared with the Musgrave manuscript. He thrust it into his pocket when Musgrave appeared.

l: the Musgrave Ritual, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: The custom required each Musgrave to submit to the catechism when he came to man's estate. Musgrave says the paper was not hidden from others.

l: mystery, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “He handed me the very paper which I have here, Watson, and this
s: The catechism gives Holmes another mystery, which he considers even more interesting than the first. Holmes suspects that solving one mystery may solve the other and plans to investigate further in Sussex.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Sherlock Holmes follows the Musgrave Ritual’s measurements from the oak and former elm at Hurlstone to the cellar beneath the old house. There he and Reginald Musgrave find Brunton’s muffler, a concealed chamber, a brass-bound box, and Brunton’s dead body. Holmes infers that Brunton and Howells opened the chamber, that Howells may have caused or concealed Brunton’s death, and that she took the box’s contents. The recovered objects are identified as the ancient crown of the Kings of England, a Royalist treasure hidden during the troubles after Charles I’s execution and intended for Charles II.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Sherlock Holmes interprets the Musgrave Ritual, uses the oak, the former elm, the sun, and the stated measurements to locate the concealed cellar chamber, and finds Brunton’s body there. He reconstructs Brunton’s investigation and probable death, identifies the recovered relic as the ancient crown of the Kings of England, and explains its historical significance to Reginald Musgrave.

l: Hurlstone, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Hurlstone is an old L-shaped building with an ancient nucleus dated by an inscription to 1607, though its beams and stonework are considered older. Its old section contains a cellar beneath a stone passage, and the estate includes the oak, the former elm, and a lake or mere.

l: the Musgrave Ritual, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The Musgrave Ritual gives directions involving an oak, an elm, measurements, cardinal directions, and a location under the old door and passage. Holmes uses it to find the cellar chamber and interprets its opening questions as referring to a crown belonging first to the dead Charles I and then to the returning Charles II.

l: Reginald Musgrave, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Reginald Musgrave brings Holmes to Hurlstone and supplies information about the oak, the former elm, and the Ritual. He helps open the cellar, recognizes Brunton’s muffler and body, identifies the coins as belonging to Charles I, and learns from Holmes that the hidden relic is the ancient crown.

l: Brunton, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Brunton, the Musgrave butler, studied the Ritual, asked about the height of the former elm, located the concealed chamber, and apparently entered it with Howells. He was found dead inside the chamber beside the opened box, with no wound or bruise indicating how he died.

l: Howells, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Howells, a maid formerly devoted to Brunton, is believed by Holmes to have helped him raise the cellar flagstone and waited above while he entered the chamber. Holmes suspects that she either allowed the support to slip or deliberately removed it, leaving Brunton trapped, and that she took or disposed of the box’s contents before disappearing.

l: oak tree (Hurlstone), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The oak tree stands in front of Hurlstone on the left side of the drive and is described as an exceptionally old and magnificent tree. Its height and position provide one of the fixed points Holmes uses to calculate the location of the Ritual’s destination.

l: elm tree (Hurlstone), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The old elm at Hurlstone had been struck by lightning and cut down about ten years before Holmes’s investigation. Its former location, its remembered height of sixty-four feet, and the direction of its shadow allow Holmes to reconstruct Brunton’s measurements.

l: Hurlstone cellar, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The cellar beneath the old passage contains a concealed chamber about seven feet deep and four feet square. Holmes and the others find the chamber recently cleared of wood, with the flagstone raised, the box opened, and Brunton’s body beside it.

l: flagstone (Hurlstone cellar), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: A large, heavy flagstone with a rusted iron ring covers the concealed chamber in the cellar. Brunton and Howells apparently used pieces of wood to hold it open, but it later closed over Brunton and became his sepulchre.

l: Brunton's muffler, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Brunton’s thick shepherd’s-check muffler is attached to the iron ring of the cellar flagstone. Reginald Musgrave recognizes it as Brunton’s, showing that Brunton had been working at the concealed opening.

l: brass-bound wooden box (Hurlstone cellar), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The brass-bound wooden box lies in the concealed chamber with its hinged lid open and an old key projecting from the lock. It contains several old metal discs or coins, while Holmes infers that its more valuable contents had been removed.

l: crown of the Kings of England, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The crown of the Kings of England is identified by Holmes as the battered, twisted relic recovered from the mere and associated with the hidden box. It is said to have great intrinsic value and greater historical importance as a relic of the royal Stuarts.

l: Charles I of England, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Charles I of England is represented in the Ritual by the phrase “His who is gone,” which Holmes interprets as referring to the period after Charles’s execution. The coins found in the box are identified by Reginald Musgrave as coins of Charles I.

l: Charles II of England, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Charles II of England is represented in the Ritual by the phrase “He who will come,” referring to his anticipated return. Holmes says the crown was intended for Charles II, though Charles did not recover it after returning.

l: Brunton's investigation, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Brunton’s investigation involved mastering the Musgrave Ritual, asking about the former elm’s height, locating the Ritual’s destination, and opening the concealed chamber. He apparently entered the chamber to retrieve the hidden treasure and was trapped inside.

l: Brunton's death, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Brunton’s body is found crouched beside the opened box in the concealed chamber after he has been dead for several days. No wound or bruise is found, and Holmes concludes that the flagstone probably closed over him after Howells assisted or abandoned him.

l: Howells's disappearance, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Howells disappears after the events in the cellar. Holmes believes she fled after taking the treasure and that she may have left England carrying the memory of Brunton’s death.

l: discovery of the crown, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The crown is discovered through Holmes’s interpretation of the Ritual, the cellar search, and the examination of the debris recovered from the mere. A dark, twisted double ring with a stone that shines after being rubbed is identified as part of the ancient crown.

l: historical identity of the crown, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: Holmes identifies the relic as the ancient crown of the Kings of England and connects it with the royal Stuarts. He infers that it was hidden by Royalists during the troubles after Charles I’s death and was meant to be recovered by Charles II.

l: Musgrave Ritual's riddle, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The Ritual’s riddle includes the questions “Whose was it?” and “Who shall have it?” with the answers “His who is gone” and “He who will come.” Holmes interprets these as references to Charles I after his execution and Charles II before his return.

l: Royalist treasure, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, “The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have
s: The Royalist treasure consisted of precious possessions hidden during the period when the Royal party was defeated or in flight, with the hope of later recovery. The treasure at Hurlstone included the ancient crown and associated metalwork and stones.

l: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
s: Sherlock Holmes, recovering from a severe illness after an international investigation, visits Reigate with Dr. Watson and stays at Colonel Hayter's house. They learn that the Acton burglary involved the theft of several unusual household items and that the Cunningham burglary has ended in the shooting death of William Kirwan. Inspector Forrester reports that the same burglar is suspected in both incidents and produces a fragment of paper found in William Kirwan's hand, bearing the hour of his death. Holmes investigates the Cunningham case, focuses on the fragment and William's letter, and asks to inspect Cunningham's house.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
s: Sherlock Holmes visits Reigate with Dr. Watson while recovering from the strain of a prolonged investigation. Although he initially agrees to rest, he becomes intensely interested in the Acton burglary and the Cunningham burglary and murder, examines the fragment of paper, visits the crime scene with Inspector Forrester, and develops theories about William Kirwan's letter and the missing portion of the note.

l: Dr. Watson, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
s: Dr. Watson goes to Lyons to care for Sherlock Holmes and then brings him to Colonel Hayter's house near Reigate for a restorative country visit. He recognizes that Holmes's interest in the Cunningham case makes it impossible for them to remain uninvolved and accompanies the investigation.

l: Colonel Hayter, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
s: Colonel Hayter hosts Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson at his bachelor house near Reigate. He tells them about the Acton burglary, discusses the Cunningham burglary and murder, and agrees to accompany Holmes, Watson, and Inspector Forrester to Cunningham's house.

l: Inspector Forrester, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
s: Inspector Forrester investigates the Acton burglary and the Cunningham burglary and murder. He tells Holmes that the burglar was seen fleeing after shooting William Kirwan, shows Holmes the fragment of paper found in Kirwan's hand, and joins Holmes in examining the crime scene and interviewing people connected with it.

l: Cunningham (Alec Cunningham's father), The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
s: Mr. Cunningham is a Justice of the Peace whose house was entered during the Cunningham burglary. He heard the alarm, saw the fleeing burglar from his bedroom window, and later showed Holmes and Inspector Forrester where the burglar crossed the garden hedge.

l: Alec Cunningham, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, VII. The Reigate Squires
s: Alec Cunningham was smoking in his dressing-gown when he heard William Kirwan calling for help. He ran downstairs, saw two men wrestling outside the open back door, and witnessed one of them shoot the other before fleeing.
